papers.version: Published Econometrica article, 2015; permission cover excluded
papers.synthesis: The historical episode supplies identifying variation rather than scenery. Exogenous-characteristic recovery is distinguished from estimation of endogenous externalities. Reduced-form reorientation, structural parameters, and counterfactual predictions occupy separate evidentiary stages.
observations: Spatial concentration alone cannot distinguish externalities from fundamentals.
Within-city estimates differ from across-city elasticities.
Institutional history explains the division's geography.
Agglomeration and dispersion forces motivate the model.
The exogenous benchmark precedes endogenous characteristics.
Composite fundamentals are defined before inversion.
Reduced-form evidence has a distinct explanatory purpose.
Additional parameters require additional identifying variation.
Commuter sorting changes the meaning of average travel times.
The ending contrasts successful and unsuccessful model variants.

papers.synthesis: A workplace-residence mechanism links history, reduced-form evidence, recursive recovery, and counterfactuals. More restrictive structural exercises enter later, with their extra assumptions stated. Absolute and proportional spatial changes are carefully distinguished.
observations: Transport costs explain why workplaces and residences separate.
Network development is tied to the historical evidence.
Additional historical records enable specification checks.
Observed and model-inferred series are separately labeled.
External validity is discussed as a separate task.
A class of models precedes a particular parametrization.
Land payments and resident/workplace income are distinguished.
Sufficiency is restricted to the stated class of models.
Absolute growth and percentage decentralization are reconciled.
Extra structure is introduced in a recursive order.
Historical recovery and policy counterfactuals are separated.
The conclusion explains the mechanism before summarizing estimates.

papers.synthesis: Commuting links explain heterogeneous local employment responses. The paper carries residence/workplace distinctions through theory, measurement, simulated shocks, and independent evidence. Geographic aggregation does not silently eliminate cross-boundary links.
observations: Worker choices motivate local employment elasticity.
A local elasticity is an endogenous heterogeneous object.
A descriptive distribution motivates the omitted linkage.
Spatial scope and land supply are introduced explicitly.
Residence and workplace choices precede mobility probabilities.
Equal expected utility does not imply equal real wages.
Initial equilibrium objects support counterfactual computation.
Estimated, assumed, and counterfactual quantities are distinguished.
A no-commuting comparison isolates an economic channel.
Controls and interactions have distinct interpretive roles.
Commuting explains why housing supply affects residence differently.
Weighting and clustering are disclosed beside heterogeneous effects.

papers.version: Published QJE article, 2020; PDF title uses Indices
papers.synthesis: The price-index argument distinguishes residual interpretations, normalization, inversion, and aggregation. Empirical comparisons isolate alternative sources of disagreement instead of changing several assumptions at once.
observations: Alternative treatments of demand residuals are distinguished.
The missing absolute taste scale is explained economically.
The expenditure function precedes its demand system.
Residuals are not automatically independently measured tastes.
Each price-index component receives an interpretation.
Demand inversion is linked to sufficient conditions.
Group-specific parameters require distinct aggregation reasoning.
Prices are linked to measured purchases and quantities.
Substitution, variety turnover, and tastes are separated.
Comparison indices isolate the source of the bias.
Normalization robustness differs from relaxing IIA.

papers.synthesis: A taxonomy of spatial ingredients precedes concrete models. Closure, ownership, spatial support, inversion, and multiplicity are treated as economic choices. Numerical illustrations remain explicitly stylized.
observations: Policy relevance motivates agglomeration and dispersion forces.
Findings are organized by mechanisms, not paper chronology.
The spatial unit changes the plausibility of trade balance.
Model properties follow named equilibrium conditions.
The stylized economy's support and mobility are declared.
Map captions disclose changes, truncation, and scales.
Unique inversion and unique equilibrium are distinguished.
Temporary shocks and permanent effects define path dependence.
Methodological and substantive insights are separated.

papers.synthesis: Concrete within-city patterns motivate an accessible model. Worker and firm choices carry the explanation with limited notation. Model variants are selected for the question and available data rather than presented as an automatic realism ladder.
observations: Specific land-use patterns motivate the model.
Units, normalization, missing areas, and sources accompany panels.
Agents and choices precede mathematical machinery.
Optimization conditions explain the inverted fundamentals.
The empirical question determines useful extensions.
External estimates are compared with spatial-scale qualifications.
A historical micro-record provides a specification check.
Complementary building investment changes infrastructure evaluation.
Reduced-form externalities do not identify their microfoundations.

papers.synthesis: The itinerary is defined early and linked to complementarity and substitution. The empirical object, computational solution, and equilibrium extension are separate contributions. Model/data comparisons label normalized quantities and scenario restrictions.
observations: The itinerary is defined through a concrete sequence of stops.
The dimensionality problem motivates importance sampling.
The comparison identifies the added travel linkage.
Geographic resolution and sample differences are disclosed.
Sequence codes and denominators are defined in notes.
Estimator choice responds to treatment heterogeneity.
Consumption access differs from conventional market access.
Daily choices are separated from residence/workplace choices.
Parameter differences receive a behavioral explanation.
Observed, predicted, and normalized quantities are labeled separately.
Additional counterfactuals distinguish sources of complementarity.
The conclusion reconnects the method to the mechanism.
